title: The In-House Counsel Movement
pub: The Practice 2, no. 4 (May–June 2016), Harvard Law School Center on the Legal Profession
author: David B. Wilkins

dup.label: is in house counsel movement going global preliminary assessment role internal counsel in emerging economies

sib.t: Is the In-House Counsel Movement Going Global? A Preliminary Assessment of the Role of Internal Counsel in Emerging Economies

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: General counsel: Strategic authority carries guardian tension
st.an: Wilkins accepts the rise of general counsel as strategic buyers, managers and governance actors, and materially develops the proposition through a six-dimensional empirical framework. He also substantiates the cluster’s central tension by distinguishing demonstrated gains in authority and status from unresolved claims about cost control, independence, law-firm displacement and future durability.

st.t: Global legal markets: Liberalization remains locally contested
st.an: The source accepts that globalization does not produce uniform convergence and materially develops the cluster’s buyer-power account: it explains how in-house counsel intensify competition among law firms while proposing a comparative framework for measuring locally adapted authority and status across jurisdictions. It treats global diffusion as an empirical question rather than an inevitable replication of the US model.
qs: At the same time, these increasingly sophisticated internal lawyers sought to break up the long-standing relationships between companies and law firms by requiring firms to compete for every new piece of significant business and choosing the winner based on the price and perceived expertise of the particular lawyers involved.
Or is it a process of adoption and adaptation, with local factors playing a significant role in determining the contours of the in-house movement in emerging economies?

st.t: Buyer authority: In-house growth need not displace firms
st.an: Wilkins directly supports the cluster’s principal distinction: in-house counsel gained authority as diagnosticians and purchasers, while departmental growth did not necessarily displace outside firms. His CPP evidence shows that the largest departments could devote a higher-than-average budget share to outside counsel, separating buyer power from external-market contraction.
qs: Lawyers in these departments now regularly perform legal work that traditionally was done by outside counsel, acting both as “diagnosticians” of their company’s legal needs and as the primary “purchasing agents” for legal services that need to be procured.
Indeed, the five largest legal departments in our sample spent a higher percentage of their legal budget on outside law firms than the average company we surveyed.

st.t: Corporate buyers: Insourcing and partnerships coexist
st.an: Wilkins directly supports the cluster’s central proposition: in-house counsel have gained control over how corporate legal work is allocated, but this has not displaced enduring law-firm relationships. He finds that transactional purchasing is overstated and that sophisticated buyers increasingly combine tighter control with concentrated preferred-provider partnerships.
qs: As a result, we concluded at the end of the CPP study that while there had been an important shift in the degree of control that internal counsel exercised over both the amount of work that is given to particular firms, as well as the manner in which that work is assigned, evaluated, and compensated, it was an exaggeration to view GCs as employing a strict “spot contracting” model for the purchase of legal services.

st.t: General counsel: Corporate leadership may weaken independence
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis’s account of a shift toward corporate leadership: it presents the GC as a central management figure while acknowledging some loss of compliance oversight. It also confirms that professional independence is a core but asserted—rather than empirically demonstrated—claim of the in-house counsel movement.
qs: Once again, what evidence we have seen since 2008 reinforces the basic trend of the GC being a central figure of the top management team in most companies; although, as a result of the crisis in some organizations, compliance no longer reports to the GC.

At the core of this project is the claim that in-house counsel are just as capable—indeed, arguably more capable—of exercising independent professional judgment than lawyers working in outside law firms.

st.t: In-house power: Business integration risks professional capture
st.an: Wilkins supports the cluster’s core account: in-house counsel have gained substantial purchasing and advisory authority, but closer integration with corporate management may compromise genuine professional independence. The source treats these risks as contested rather than proving capture and does not materially develop the cluster’s reciprocal-duty or contextual-regulation proposals.
qs: Lawyers in these departments now regularly perform legal work that traditionally was done by outside counsel, acting both as “diagnosticians” of their company’s legal needs and as the primary “purchasing agents” for legal services that need to be procured.

Instead of seeing themselves as “independent professionals,” Rosen argued that the growing integration of in-house lawyers into cross functional project teams designed to work more closely with business leaders threatened to turn the in-house lawyer into just another “consultant” who values the “appearance of ‘independence’” as opposed to any real commitment to public purposes or detachment from client aims.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source indirectly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: technology may standardize and reallocate parts of legal work and alter in-house structures, but predictions of wholesale professional displacement are treated cautiously. Its evidence is historical and does not substantively address current task-level AI capability, verification or deployment design.
qs: Needless to say, these are large and difficult questions, and prior reports of the demise of lawyers as independent professionals have proven to be significantly exaggerated for both in-house and outside counsel.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source broadly supports the cluster’s cautious account: standardised technology may substitute for customised handling of routine legal problems and reshape in-house departments, but these effects remain predictions rather than proof of wholesale professional displacement. It does not materially develop the cluster’s pricing, workflow-allocation, training or verification analysis.
qs: Needless to say, these are large and difficult questions, and prior reports of the demise of lawyers as independent professionals have proven to be significantly exaggerated for both in-house and outside counsel.

kp.k: In-house expansion rests on three contested justifications
kp.d: This historical account describes the growth of U.S. in-house counsel rather than measuring AI adoption. Wilkins identifies three arguments advanced by movement proponents since the 1980s: internal lawyers reduce costs, provide better advice through business knowledge, and better protect corporate citizenship and long-term values. These are proponents’ justifications, not independently established findings of superior cost-effectiveness or independence.
qs: Starting in the 1980s, GCs in large companies began to make three distinct claims about the market for corporate legal services that justified increasing the power, authority, and standing of their position.
Proponents of the inside counsel movement argued their advice was not only more economical but also better.
As a result, GCs argued that they should be entrusted with the role of being both a “partner” to the business and the “guardian” of the company’s long-term reputation and values.

kp.k: Six dimensions assess transformation beyond department size
kp.d: Wilkins proposes assessing size, credentials and demographics, control over outside counsel, internal authority, professional standing, and public-policy influence. He reports U.S. progress on all six, while treating their continued development after the global financial crisis as an empirical question. Conversations with hundreds of GCs, including more than 250 CLOs attending Harvard’s Leadership in Corporate Counsel course, are offered as support for the framework’s continuing relevance, not as a replacement longitudinal survey.
qs: Together, these metrics of change provide an important tool for evaluating and benchmarking in-house legal departments vis-à-vis their parent companies, their outside service providers (e.g., law firms), and the legal profession as a whole.
In the United States, there is strong evidence that legal departments have changed on all six of these dimensions in line with the tenets of the in-house counsel movement.

kp.k: Purchasing evidence provides a pre-crisis baseline
kp.d: The Corporate Purchasing Project sidebar describes research conducted in 2006–2007 involving 166 S&P 500 CLOs, written survey data from 139 companies, and in-depth interview responses from 43 companies across manufacturing and services. Separately, the narrative says more than 50 GCs were interviewed. The research examined provider quality assessment, purchasing, management, and relationship termination; Wilkins explicitly qualifies its applicability after 2008 and proposes new research rather than presenting post-crisis comparisons as measured results.
qs: The project included surveys and interviews of 166 CLOs of S&P 500 companies—nearly one-third of the total.
The data set comprised both written survey data from 139 companies and in-depth interview responses from 43 companies spread across a diverse range of manufacturing and service sectors.
Going forward, the data offers a pre-GFC snapshot and baseline for determining how much has—or hasn’t—changed in the structures and operations of in-house legal departments in the intervening years.

kp.k: Department size poorly predicts power or outside spending
kp.d: CPP departments had a median of 35 lawyers but ranged from almost wholly outsourced functions to more than 1,000 lawyers. The five largest departments devoted a greater share of their legal budgets to outside firms than the average respondent. Financial-services departments were often large but performed routine transaction and compliance work, and their GCs were less likely to report directly to CEOs. Post-2008 divergence in department size is presented as anecdotal, not systematic evidence.
qs: Thus, while the median legal department employed 35 lawyers, the range in size was quite significant, with some companies having almost completely outsourced their legal function and others maintaining legal departments of more than 1,000 lawyers.
Indeed, the five largest legal departments in our sample spent a higher percentage of their legal budget on outside law firms than the average company we surveyed.
Nor is size a perfect proxy for the importance of the work that is done by internal counsel, or their importance within the corporate hierarchy.

kp.k: In-house prestige changed recruitment and gender representation
kp.d: Wilkins describes rising credentials and recruitment from leading firms, while noting most GC offices still did not recruit directly from law school. He cites a 2015 Minority Corporate Counsel Association report that women held 25 percent of Fortune 500 GC positions. He proposes that more welcoming working environments, advocacy by senior women, corporate diversity priorities, and independent reasons to elevate GCs jointly explain rising female representation alongside increasing prestige. Whether this pattern would survive tighter budgets and greater male interest remained an open research question.
qs: Although most GC offices still do not recruit directly from law school, they now have their pick of talented midlevel associates and junior partners from the best law firms, with senior in-house lawyers frequently recruited from the top ranks of the partnerships of outside firms.

But as in-house legal departments have become increasingly feminized, they have *gained* in status both within the company and in the legal profession as a whole, and the financial rewards have increased as well.

kp.k: Outside counsel relationships resisted transactional purchasing
kp.d: The movement sought competitive purchasing organized around individual lawyers rather than durable firm relationships, but CPP evidence showed incomplete control. About 20 percent of GCs frequently terminated an important firm relationship within the preceding three years; more than 30 percent never did, and almost 50 percent did so once or twice. Departments with 26 to 100 lawyers were most willing to terminate relationships; very large departments were no more likely than small ones to do so. Outside spending continued rising through the 1990s and first decade of the 21st century, and extensive monitoring did not increase satisfaction.
qs: According to the CPP study, for example, only about 20 percent of GCs from S&P 500 companies reported terminating an important law firm relationship frequently within the last three years; more than 30 percent had never done so; and almost 50 percent had done so only once or twice.
Similarly, the extensive monitoring and controlling of law firms did not result in increased levels of client satisfaction.
Relationships at the firm level still mattered.

kp.d: Based on his experience with GCs since 2008, rather than a new systematic survey, Wilkins argues that tighter fee control had not substantially increased firm terminations. He describes consolidation of spending among preferred firms in exchange for discounts and investment. Whether consultants and other non-law-firm providers would disrupt those relationships was reserved for CPP2 investigation.
qs: Although companies have attempted to exert even greater control over outside counsel fees since the GFC, this has not caused them to terminate law firm relationships more frequently than they did before the crisis.

If anything, companies are insisting even more on a “partnering” model with their primary external providers in which these increasingly sophisticated and price-sensitive consumers concentrate the bulk of their legal spend in a relatively small number of “preferred providers” in return for discounts and other forms of investment by the law firm—discounts and investments that firms are even more willing to give than before 2008 in order to keep the work.

kp.k: General counsel gained broad corporate leadership authority
kp.d: Almost 90 percent of CPP GCs reported directly to the CEO; many also managed public relations, government affairs, human resources, or compliance. Wilkins describes an ambition to integrate legal and business considerations throughout corporate decision-making. Subsequent observations reinforced this leadership trend, although compliance had ceased reporting to the GC in some organizations after the crisis.
qs: Thus, in the CPP we found the overwhelming majority—almost 90 percent—of the GCs in our sample reported directly to the CEO.
Many also oversaw other related corporate functions, such as public relations, government affairs, human resources, and compliance.

And virtually all were working to convince corporate leaders that their companies should move beyond a culture of “legal compliance” to one in which the goal is to create a “legally astute organization” where legal and business considerations are integrated at every level of the organization.

kp.k: Professional independence remains disputed despite rising status
kp.d: Wilkins presents professional independence as a central movement claim, supported institutionally by the corporate counsel association. He reports critics’ concerns after Enron and the financial crisis that dependence on employers undermines gatekeeping, including proposals for GCs to report solely to an independent board committee. He also describes European privilege restrictions as evidence of resistance to employed lawyers’ independence claims, noting challenges by some member states and national courts rather than a uniform European position.
qs: At the core of this project is the claim that in-house counsel are just as capable—indeed, arguably more capable—of exercising independent professional judgment than lawyers working in outside law firms.

Indeed, some have gone so far as to argue that GCs should be removed from the control of corporate managers and report only to an independent committee of the company’s board to ensure true independence.
At the core of this decision is a fundamental doubt about whether employed lawyers can ever truly be independent.

kp.k: Corporate counsel influence regulation through advocacy and private ordering
kp.d: The article describes ACC advocacy on multidisciplinary and multijurisdictional practice and Dodd-Frank whistle-blowing provisions. It also argues that multinational GCs effectively make policy where legal standards are ambiguous or contradictory, using third-party supplier child-labor standards as an example. The asserted influence of corporate policy and enforcement on real outcomes is Wilkins’s argument, not a quantified comparative finding.
qs: For many important policy issues facing global companies—for example, the question of child labor standards for third-party suppliers in countries such as India and China—relevant legal standards are likely to be ill-defined, under- or overinclusive, or contradictory.
In such cases, it is often up to the GC to craft a policy within these broad constraints that is consistent with both the company’s economic interests and its values.

kp.k: Global diffusion entails local adaptation rather than uniformity
kp.d: Wilkins describes the movement’s expansion into the United Kingdom and Europe since the turn of the 21st century, encouraged by complex regulation, corporate scandals, and the spread of U.S.-style firms. He nevertheless emphasizes economic, political, and cultural differences and presents adoption versus imitation in emerging economies as a research question. Preliminary India and Brazil research suggests potentially greater differences, not demonstrated global convergence.
qs: Although many of the six variables described above can be found in the internal legal departments of large U.K. and European corporations, there remain essential differences that are arguably based on important economic, political, and cultural differences between Europe and the United States.

Is it a story of dispersion, with societies merely mimicking the process as it developed in the United States? Or is it a process of adoption and adaptation, with local factors playing a significant role in determining the contours of the in-house movement in emerging economies?

kp.k: Business integration may weaken independent professional identity
kp.d: Wilkins reports Rosen’s 2002 follow-up to his earlier departmental research: some formerly transformed departments had been reengineered, and cross-functional project teams threatened to recast independent professionals as business consultants. This concern is attributed to Rosen, not presented as a demonstrated consequence of AI or a universal trajectory. Wilkins cautions that previous predictions of lawyers’ professional demise had been exaggerated.
qs: Instead of seeing themselves as “independent professionals,” Rosen argued that the growing integration of in-house lawyers into cross functional project teams designed to work more closely with business leaders threatened to turn the in-house lawyer into just another “consultant” who values the “appearance of ‘independence’” as opposed to any real commitment to public purposes or detachment from client aims.

Needless to say, these are large and difficult questions, and prior reports of the demise of lawyers as independent professionals have proven to be significantly exaggerated for both in-house and outside counsel.

kp.k: Standardized technology could erode in-house lawyers’ power
kp.d: The article’s directly technology-related mechanism is a prediction attributed to Larry Ribstein in 2012: process-based products and services could replace customized advice for standard legal problems and weaken internal lawyers’ authority. It is not evidence of realized AI displacement. Wilkins proposes further empirical research on technology, diversity, and sourcing, segmentation, and unbundling of legal work to understand how departments change.
qs: At the same time, the late Larry Ribstein argued in 2012 that in a world in which “smart” technology will increasingly allow companies to develop process-based solutions to many standard legal problems, “in-house lawyers ultimately may find their own power eroded by products and services that replace customized legal advice with standardized technology.”

In addition to revisiting the core questions we investigated in the CPP, this research will also probe the extent to which in-house legal departments are leading the charge for change within the profession, whether concerning the use of new disruptive technologies within in-house departments, innovative diversity and inclusion programs, and/or the use of pioneering new ways of sourcing, segmenting, and unbundling legal work.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article makes no explicit AI-specific claim. Its closest relevant claim concerns the possibility that standardized technology could substitute for customized legal advice and diminish in-house lawyers’ authority.
pts.d: Wilkins presents technology-driven erosion of in-house counsel’s power as an unresolved possibility, not an established outcome. He introduces the specific substitution mechanism through a discussion of Larry Ribstein’s 2012 argument; it is a quoted antecedent, not an independently demonstrated finding by Wilkins. Wilkins’s own framing is that greater technology use, alongside integration into cross-functional business teams, may threaten earlier gains in internal counsel’s standing. The source does not identify this technology as AI or describe particular AI capabilities.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The technology-related proposition rests on cited scholarly argument and an open research question, not measured technology effects.
pts.d: Wilkins cites Ribstein’s argument as the basis for the technology-substitution scenario. The article’s Corporate Purchasing Project provides empirical background on in-house departments, but its 2006–2007 data do not establish AI or technology-driven displacement. Wilkins proposes subsequent research to investigate disruptive technologies and changes in legal departments. No AI benchmarks, deployment cases, productivity measurements, or measured displacement effects are offered.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The outlook is open-ended from the article’s 2016 perspective and explicitly qualified.
pts.d: The article considers changes since the 2008 financial crisis and possible further changes in the coming years, without a forecast date or adoption threshold. The substitution scenario depends on technology enabling process-based solutions to standard legal problems. Wilkins cautions that earlier predictions of lawyers’ loss of professional independence have been exaggerated. This is a conditional possibility rather than a prediction of inevitable replacement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected segment is corporate in-house legal departments, particularly their lawyers’ authority, professional standing, and provision of advice on standard legal problems.
pts.d: The discussion concerns the buyer side of corporate legal services: GCs, CLOs, internal lawyers, and their corporate employers. Companies could obtain standardized, process-based solutions in place of some customized legal advice, potentially weakening internal lawyers’ power. Wilkins also anticipates continued evolution in departmental roles and structures, but does not quantify staffing reductions, cost savings, or effects on outside providers attributable to technology. No access-to-justice or public-facing AI-service claim is made.
